clue.text: The go-ahead for rerouting a trench cable ?

indicators.note: rerouting sends something along a new path, so the letters of the cable phrase are laid out afresh

explanation.surface: Permission is given to divert a cable running through a trench.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rerouting' is the anagram signal working on all twelve letters of 'a trench cable'.
explanation.definitionFit: A free hand to act as one likes is unrestricted permission, the go-ahead.

clue.text: It could be a nice day for breathing one's last?

indicators.note: says the letters of the phrase could be rearranged into something else

explanation.surface: Someone sees a fine day as a good day to die.
explanation.walkthrough: 'could be' signals the anagram of 'nice day'; the poison is a means for breathing one's last.
explanation.definitionFit: A deadly poison, notorious for fast fatal effect, is a means of dying.

clue.text: Salesman the Spanish drive off ?

parts.note: a rep is a sales representative
el is Spanish for 'the'

explanation.surface: A Spanish salesman drives away.
explanation.definitionFit: To repel is to force back or ward off, driving an attacker away.

clue.text: Is a friend in France clear where he can get a drink?.

definitions.text: where he can get a drink

parts.note: est is French for 'is', as 'in France' says
ami is French for a friend, signalled by 'in France'
net means clear, as in net profit after deductions

explanation.surface: A man asks whether a friend in France can see his way to a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in France' turns 'Is' and 'a friend' into French, EST and AMI; 'clear' is net profit.
explanation.definitionFit: An estaminet is a small French cafe or bar, a place to buy a drink.

clue.text: Hear the roll, please

definitions.meaning: in old usage '...' means listen or hear
a roll is a register of names, a catalogue
in archaic use '...' means to please or choose, as in 'the wind bloweth where it listeth'

explanation.surface: A teacher asks the class to listen to the register being called.
explanation.definitionFit: Three senses: archaic listen, a register of names, and archaic wish or choose.

clue.text: He related how the island rose to the right

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means reading the island name upwards, so backwards

parts.note: Arran is an island off south-west Scotland in the Firth of Clyde

explanation.surface: Someone tells how an island emerged from the sea on the right.
explanation.walkthrough: ARRAN, a Scottish island, read upwards for 'rose' gives NARRA, then TO and R.
explanation.definitionFit: A storyteller is someone who relates or recounts events.

clue.text: Rhoda's hidden stock

indicators.note: hidden here means disguised, so the name is rearranged out of recognition

parts.note: the 's only shows possession or stands for 'is', so it adds no letters: the word before it gives these letters as it is written

explanation.surface: Rhoda keeps a secret supply tucked away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hidden' looks like a hidden-word signal, but no run of letters gives the answer; it disguises 'Rhoda' as an anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoard is a stored-up stock of valuables or supplies.

clue.text: Argumentative type may make moving speeches

definitions.text: Argumentative type may make moving speeches

parts.words: Argumentative type may make moving speeches
parts.note: people who argue in formal contests make speeches on motions, so 'moving' means proposing a motion

explanation.surface: Quarrelsome people can be stirring orators.
explanation.walkthrough: 'moving' seems to mean emotionally stirring, but in formal debate one moves a motion.
explanation.definitionFit: People who argue a motion in formal contests are those who propose and oppose it.

clue.text: A visitor fresh from Scotland

definitions.meaning: someone who calls at a house
in Scots, '...' means fresh, as of fish or air

explanation.surface: A newcomer who has just arrived from Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who calls at your door is a visitor; in Scottish dialect the word also means fresh.

clue.text: Mouth watering sherry perhaps

parts.note: something that makes the mouth water before a meal, of which a glass of sherry is a typical example

explanation.surface: A tasting note praising a delicious sherry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mouth watering' reads as praise of the sherry, but it describes the job of a pre-dinner drink: to whet the appetite.
explanation.definitionFit: A pre-dinner drink such as dry sherry is taken to stimulate hunger before the meal.

clue.text: The Scots are not in this sphere of action

parts.note: taken as written
in Scots dialect 'not' is said and written na, which 'The Scots' signals

explanation.surface: A remark that Scotsmen do not belong in some field of activity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Scots are not' is the Scots phrase 'are na', run together.
explanation.definitionFit: An arena is a field of contest or activity, figuratively any scene where action takes place.

clue.text: How poets light up

parts.note: the poetic, archaic verb poets use for 'illuminate'

explanation.surface: A question about how poets brighten or kindle their lamps.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue asks for the word poets use meaning 'light up', a shortened literary form of illuminate.
explanation.definitionFit: The literary verb is a poetic shortening of illuminate, meaning to cast light on.

clue.text: Hold on to this — worth two in the bus'?

definitions.text: Hold on to this — worth two in the bus'?

parts.words: Hold on to this — worth two in the bus'?
parts.note: a rail for gripping, with the proverb 'a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush' altered to a bus

explanation.surface: Advice to grip something on a bus, echoing a proverb.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush' becomes 'worth two in the bus', pointing to the hand and to the rail a passenger grips.
explanation.definitionFit: A rail fitted for passengers to grip, as on buses and stairs, is held with the hand.

clue.text: Two notes to utter for relaxation

parts.note: E is a musical note
A is a musical note
to sing is to utter in song

explanation.surface: Playing a couple of notes and singing as a way of unwinding.
explanation.definitionFit: Loosening or lessening tension is a slackening, a relaxation.

clue.text: The branch post office girl gets a writ

parts.note: sub as in sub-branch or subsidiary office
Ena is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A girl at the local branch post office is served legal papers.
explanation.definitionFit: A legal summons ordering attendance in court is a kind of writ.

clue.text: To renounce on oath could be far worse

indicators.note: says the letters of the phrase could be rearranged into another word

explanation.surface: Swearing off something under oath could make things far worse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'could be' tells you 'far worse' is to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: To abjure or give up something solemnly, under oath, is to swear it off.

clue.text: Fellows, mainly

parts.note: 'mainly' means on the main, at sea, so the fellows are sailors serving together

explanation.surface: A note that something applies chiefly to fellows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mainly' looks like 'mostly' but means 'on the main', the open sea, so these are companions aboard ship.
explanation.definitionFit: Sailors serving on the same vessel are companions, fellows at sea.

clue.text: Not the principal way to attribute the designing of London's Law Courts

parts.note: 'by' is the word used to credit a work to its maker

parts.words: the designing of London's Law Courts
parts.note: G. E. Street was the architect of the Royal Courts of Justice in London

explanation.surface: An aside about crediting the design of the Royal Courts of Justice.
explanation.walkthrough: The Royal Courts of Justice in the Strand were designed by George Edmund Street, so the Law Courts are 'by Street'.
explanation.definitionFit: A side road, as opposed to a main thoroughfare, is a minor route.

clue.text: Robert's leave's cancelled-you know the ropes

parts.note: Bob is short for Robert
if leave is cancelled one stays; 's here is 'is'

explanation.surface: Robert's leave is called off, and he is a seasoned sailor who knows the ropes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Robert's' gives BOB with the 's as a link; 'leave's cancelled' reads 'leave is cancelled', so he STAYS.
explanation.definitionFit: These are the ropes or chains holding a ship's bowsprit down to the stem, nautical rigging.

clue.text: Sound of gunfire leads to the French army decoration?

parts.note: a bang is the noise of a gun
le is French for 'the'

explanation.surface: Gunfire leads to a French military medal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'army' is read as arm-y: a bangle is an ornament for the arm, not a military medal.
explanation.definitionFit: A rigid bracelet worn round the arm is an ornament for that limb.

clue.text: The curse of drink, so pronounced by the drunkard ?

definitions.text: The curse of drink, so pronounced by the drunkard ?

parts.words: The curse of drink, so pronounced by the drunkard ?
parts.note: a drunkard slurring 'curse' produces the sound of a cherry spirit, which is itself a drink

explanation.surface: A temperance warning about the evils of alcohol.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The curse of drink' sounds like a sermon, but a drunk slurring 'curse' says the name of a cherry brandy.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is a clear brandy distilled from cherries, a strong drink.

clue.text: Moorish fashion in Yorkshire?

parts.note: the Yorkshire song 'On Ilkla Moor Baht 'at' is about going on the moor with no headgear

explanation.surface: A question about North African styles in a northern English county.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moorish' suggests the Moors of North Africa, but refers to Ilkley Moor; the Yorkshire folk song 'On Ilkla Moor Baht 'at' means 'on Ilkley Moor without a hat'.
explanation.definitionFit: Going bareheaded, without any headgear, is the style the song describes.

clue.text: Are you the new convert, honey pet ?

indicators.note: the question asks whether the endearment, rearranged, is the convert, inviting a reshuffle of its letters

explanation.surface: Someone asks their sweetheart whether they have just joined the faith.
explanation.walkthrough: 'honey pet' is an endearment in the surface, but its eight letters are what 'Are you ...?' asks to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A recent convert to a religion, or any beginner, is a novice in the faith.

clue.text: Oddly enough, where women wear the trousers

definitions.text: Oddly enough, where women wear the trousers

parts.words: Oddly enough, where women wear the trousers
parts.note: women's quarters in a Muslim household, whose name is also given to baggy trousers, though the idiom says women are in charge

explanation.surface: A household where, strangely, the women are the bosses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wear the trousers' idiomatically means to be in charge; here the women literally wear baggy pants named after the women's quarters, where men rule.
explanation.definitionFit: The secluded women's quarters of a Muslim household gave their name to loose gathered trousers.

clue.text: One thousand, some give

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
M is the Roman numeral for a thousand
some of something is a part of it

explanation.surface: Someone gives part of a thousand pounds.
explanation.definitionFit: To impart is to bestow or give, as with knowledge or a share.

clue.text: A truly promising Scottish lass

parts.note: in the Scottish song '... Laurie', she 'gave me her promise true'

explanation.surface: A Scottish girl full of potential.
explanation.walkthrough: 'truly promising' suggests a girl with prospects, but recalls the line 'gave me her promise true' from the Scottish song 'Annie Laurie'.
explanation.definitionFit: The heroine of the song 'Annie Laurie' is the Scottish girl who made a true promise.

clue.text: Bookie very happy, taking in Russian capital

indicators.note: the words take the city inside them, a run spanning the join

explanation.surface: A bookmaker is delighted to accept Russian money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'capital' suggests money, but it is a capital city, held across the words 'Bookie very'; it was the capital of medieval Kievan Rus.
explanation.definitionFit: The city was the seat of medieval Kievan Rus and later capital of the Ukrainian Soviet republic.

clue.text: Ship one found in an old railway

indicators.note: the single letter is found inside the railway's initials

parts.note: LNER was the London and North Eastern Railway, a British company before 1948 nationalisation
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A ship turns up on a disused railway line.
explanation.walkthrough: LNER, the London and North Eastern Railway, was one of Britain's pre-war railway companies.
explanation.definitionFit: An ocean passenger vessel on a regular route is a large ship.

clue.text: Hamlet questioned its advisability

parts.note: Hamlet's soliloquy 'To be, or not to be' asks whether going on living is wise

explanation.surface: A remark about Shakespeare's Prince of Denmark doubting whether something was wise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hamlet' looks like a small village, but it is Shakespeare's prince, whose 'To be, or not to be' questions being itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Being alive, the state of being, is what 'to be' refers to.

clue.text: They sound the most inane chatterers

definitions.text: They sound the most inane chatterers

parts.words: They sound the most inane chatterers
parts.note: the proverb '... make the most sound' is used of foolish talkers

explanation.surface: A description of the silliest gossips.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb that hollow pots ring loudest is applied to people who talk much and know little; 'sound' is both making noise and seeming.
explanation.definitionFit: Hollow containers ring loudest, as the proverb says of foolish people who talk most.
